interactions.label: Which stage in the WHO xerophthalmia classification represents an irreversible c

params.question: Which stage in the WHO xerophthalmia classification represents an irreversible change leading to permanent blindness?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Night blindness is the earliest sign and is fully reversible with Vitamin A supplementation, as rhodopsin production in the retina resumes once stores are replenished.
Bitot's spots — foamy, triangular patches on the conjunctiva — are a hallmark sign of Vitamin A deficiency but are still reversible with supplementation.
Corneal xerosis causes haziness and dryness of the cornea. While serious, it can still respond to urgent Vitamin A therapy if treated before structural breakdown occurs.
Correct. Keratomalacia involves softening and structural breakdown of the cornea, causing permanent blindness. Unlike earlier stages that respond to Vitamin A, this damage is irreversible.

overallFeedback.feedback: In the WHO classification, night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and even early corneal xerosis can respond to Vitamin A therapy. Keratomalacia (X3B) — where the cornea softens and disintegrates — is the irreversible end-stage that leads to permanent blindness.

The xerophthalmia classification moves from fully reversible stages (night blindness, Bitot's spots) to irreversible corneal destruction (keratomalacia). Recognising this progression is key to intervening before permanent damage occurs.

params.question: A 3-month-old infant presents with hypocalcaemic seizures, while an 18-month-old presents with bow legs. Both are diagnosed with nutritional rickets. What best explains the different clinical presentations?

answers.text: The 3-month-old has a more severe form of rickets than the 18-month-old

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The difference is not about severity. Both may have equally severe rickets, but different skeletal regions grow fastest at different ages, so the same disease manifests differently.

answers.text: Different parts of the skeleton are growing fastest at different ages

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rickets affects whichever bones are growing fastest. In early infancy, skull changes (craniotabes) and hypocalcaemia (seizures) dominate. Once weight-bearing begins around 12–18 months, softened lower-limb bones bend, producing bow legs.

answers.text: The 3-month-old has Vitamin D–resistant rickets, while the 18-month-old has nutritional rickets

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Different aetiologies are not needed to explain these presentations. Nutritional rickets alone produces age-dependent clinical patterns because skeletal growth is not uniform across infancy and childhood.

answers.text: Bow legs develop only after growth plate fusion, which occurs after one year of age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Growth plates do not fuse during infancy or early childhood. Bow legs result from unmineralised, softened bone bending under the mechanical stress of weight-bearing, which begins when the child starts to walk.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle is age-dependent skeletal involvement. Rickets affects whichever bones are growing fastest: skull changes dominate in early infancy, chest deformities appear in the first year, and lower-limb bowing emerges once the child bears weight.

Rickets is a single disease with age-dependent presentation: skull in early infancy, chest in the first year, and lower limbs once weight-bearing begins. A systematic head-to-toe examination is essential to catch the full picture.

interactions.label: A well-nourished 20-month-old child with no signs of Vitamin A deficiency is bro

params.question: A well-nourished 20-month-old child with no signs of Vitamin A deficiency is brought for a routine immunisation visit. According to India's national programme, what Vitamin A supplementation should be given?

answers.text: No supplementation — Vitamin A is only given to children with clinical deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: India's national programme provides universal Vitamin A prophylaxis to all children under 5 years, not just those with clinical deficiency. This mass supplementation reduces all-cause under-5 mortality by approximately 23–24%.

answers.text: 2,00,000 IU orally on Day 1, Day 2, and Day 14

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This three-dose schedule (Day 1, 2, and 14) is the therapeutic protocol for confirmed Vitamin A deficiency, not the routine prophylaxis schedule. A well-nourished child without deficiency needs only the single prophylactic dose.

answers.text: 2,00,000 IU orally now, repeated every 6 months until age 5

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. From 18 months onward, the prophylactic dose is 2,00,000 IU every six months until age 5. The first dose at 9 months is smaller (1,00,000 IU) because a younger infant's liver has limited storage capacity.

answers.text: 1,00,000 IU orally, since the full dose is only for children above 3 years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 1,00,000 IU dose is given at the 9-month visit only. From 18 months onward, regardless of age within the under-5 window, the prophylactic dose is 2,00,000 IU every six months.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct prophylactic dose for a 20-month-old is 2,00,000 IU orally, repeated every 6 months until age 5. Do not confuse this with the three-dose therapeutic schedule (Day 1, 2, and 14), which is reserved for confirmed Vitamin A deficiency.

India's national programme gives 2,00,000 IU of Vitamin A every 6 months to all children from 18 months to 5 years. The first dose at 9 months is smaller (1,00,000 IU) to match the younger infant's hepatic storage capacity.

interactions.label: In megaloblastic anaemia, giving folic acid alone is safe because it corrects bo

params.question: In megaloblastic anaemia, giving folic acid alone is safe because it corrects both the haematological and neurological manifestations of Vitamin B12 deficiency.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. While folic acid does correct the megaloblastic anaemia, it does NOT address the neurological damage of B12 deficiency. Only B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, and giving folate alone masks the haematological warning signs while nerve damage continues unchecked.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Folic acid corrects the megaloblastic blood picture in both folate and B12 deficiency, but it does NOT prevent subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord caused by B12 deficiency. Giving folate alone masks the anaemia while neurological damage progresses silently.

interactions.label: A child being treated for tuberculosis with isoniazid develops refractory seizur

params.question: A child being treated for tuberculosis with isoniazid develops refractory seizures. Which mechanism best explains this complication?

answers.text: Isoniazid depletes hepatic thiamine stores, causing Wernicke's encephalopathy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Isoniazid does not primarily affect thiamine metabolism. Wernicke's encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion — a different clinical picture from isolated seizures.

answers.text: Isoniazid blocks the enzyme needed to convert pyridoxine to its active form, causing B6 deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Isoniazid inhibits pyridoxal phosphokinase, preventing activation of pyridoxine (Vitamin B6). Active B6 is essential for GABA synthesis in the brain, and its deficiency lowers the seizure threshold. This is why pyridoxine is co-prescribed with isoniazid in children.

answers.text: Isoniazid damages the terminal ileum, impairing Vitamin B12 absorption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Isoniazid does not damage the terminal ileum. Terminal ileum disease (as in Crohn's) or surgical resection impairs B12 absorption. It is metformin, not isoniazid, that reduces ileal B12 uptake.

answers.text: Isoniazid binds niacin in the gut, producing pellagra with neurological involvement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While isoniazid can rarely cause pellagra through its effect on tryptophan-to-niacin conversion, seizures are not the typical pellagra presentation. The far more common and immediate isoniazid–nutrient interaction is blocking B6 activation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Isoniazid blocks activation of pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) by inhibiting pyridoxal phosphokinase. Since active B6 is essential for GABA synthesis in the brain, its deficiency lowers the seizure threshold. This is why pyridoxine supplementation is mandatory alongside isoniazid.

Isoniazid inhibits the enzyme that activates pyridoxine (B6), which is essential for GABA synthesis. The resulting B6 deficiency lowers the seizure threshold, making pyridoxine co-prescription mandatory in children on anti-tubercular therapy.
